preference_rationale: We do not actually have ground truth labels here, so it is hard to set up an experiment like B's. Identification in this setting is judgement-based matching of data observations against real-world knowledge - less statistical in nature - and A is better suited to it. It should also not require any survey work: the institutions are prominent enough that an independent research subagent should unearth identifying geographic and demographic properties that are visible in our data, and A should be able to get to an individual bank name for at least some of the clusters. Neither plan is very good, which is why the call is weak.
critique_A:
The naming step is not the evidence-based identification this task needs. A ranks IDs by panel customer count against institutions ranked by market share and runs a Hungarian assignment on rank distance, accepting on rank agreement and a preset margin. That is size-ordering, and it inherits panel skew directly - A's own pitfalls note the panel over-represents young, urban, digital and multi-banked customers, which makes rank-by-panel-count a biased proxy for market rank. The plan should instead match observed geographic and demographic properties against researched real-world properties of prominent institutions, which needs no survey.

A has no external ground truth, so its gates measure whether clusters are stable rather than whether the names are right. It flags this itself but never resolves it.

A stable cluster that cannot be identified is not a Type I failure - that is a Type II miss, and A's tiering handles it correctly by leaving those at country and archetype rather than forcing a name.
critique_B: The one good thing B does is narrow down to an individual ticker, and that is really the only good thing it does. Everything else is disproportionate to the setting. It requires ground truth labels that do not exist here and manufactures them through a consented survey of 500 respondents per country plus provider-revealed seeds - work this desk cannot commission and should not need. The anchor stack behind it (five national regulators, OSM branch tags, published tariff schedules, benefit calendars keyed to national numbering systems) is a standing maintenance burden for a three-person data team, and putting GDPR clearance as gate zero means the project can die before producing anything.
why_loser_was_defensible: B narrows to an individual ticker, which is ultimately what the desk needs, and it is the only one of the two that attaches a calibrated confidence to a name. An analyst who weighted that above the cost of assembling ground truth would have taken B.
